newsitem.title: INDIA: Fear and trembling driving India to new coalition.
newsitem.headline: Fear and trembling driving India to new coalition.

text.p: Fear of elections could drive India's estranged political leaders together in a new coalition, but the government would be short-lived and probably opt for polls in only a few months' time, analysts said on Sunday.
No sooner had India's parliament thrown out Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda than leaders of his United Front and rival Congress party stepped up efforts to avoid mid-term polls.

Rumblings of discontent within Congress, which provoked Deve Gowda's downfall by revoking its support, pointed to a possible reconciliation with the caretaker prime minister's alliance, analysts said.
The motivation was fear and trembling, not principles, as politicians realised a dispirited electorate could punish them if polls were held now, only a year after they last voted.
"At the moment the bottom line is how to save this government because if there is an election, these people get wiped out," said Vinod Mehta, editor of Outlook magazine.
The United Front and Congress were effectively given nearly two weeks to swallow their collective pride and strike a new power-sharing deal.

President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who under the constitution will name the next prime minister, agreed on Saturday that parliament would take up the 1997/98 (April-March) budget in a special session from April 21 to 23.
That almost guarantees that political manoeuvring and brinksmanship will carry on for another 10 days.
After helping summarily dismiss Deve Gowda, some Congress deputies had second thoughts about the timing of the move prompted by party president Sitaram Kesri.

"Kesri has turned the party into a terminally ill patient on the death bed," Congress leader A.R. Antulay said. "The time has come when Congress MPs will have to strike at the root of the evil and rejuvenate the party."

Congress, which suffered its worst defeat ever in last year's general election, knows it could be badly punished in fresh polls which could bolster the United Front and, more especially, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Deve Gowda stood by his conviction that snap polls were inevitable now that his make-or-break ally Congress had turned on him. But many leaders in his 15-party United Front were not keen to face the electorate now, even if the alliance's foreign and economic accomplishments would be a campaign advantage.

"The United Front realises that an election would be unpopular with the people," said Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research, an independent think tank. "The Front would pay a smaller price than Congress, but they would rather let a few months more pass and then call for an election."

Mehta predicted the United Front would eventually persuade Deve Gowda to relinquish leadership of the coalition in the interest of forming a new government headed by the alliance. "People will feel sorry for Deve Gowda, but they are not going to let him prevent the formation of a government," he said.

Deve Gowda, according to Chopra, would like to push his popular, investor-friendly budget through parliament before stepping aside. He could remain in charge of the United Front's decision-making Steering Committee and even chair a proposed policy coordination committee with Congress.
The BJP, although the biggest party in the 542-member lower house with 162 deputies, could only watch from the margins as the United Front and Congress patched up their differences.

A new United Front-led government, with Congress either in the cabinet or supporting it from outside, would take power -- but probably not for long. "Whoever comes to power will only be there for a short time," a Western diplomat said.
"The government will survive from month to month," Mehta said. "If it gets three, four, five months more, the United Front will be quite happy with that."
Asked when elections could come, Chopra said: "Towards the end of the year."
